## Description

Newton interpolation represents the interpolating polynomial in divided-difference form,

$$
P_n(x)=a_0 + a_1(x-x_0)+a_2(x-x_0)(x-x_1)+\cdots+a_n\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(x-x_j),
$$

where $a_k=f[x_0,\ldots,x_k]$ are divided differences. For the same nodes and data, Newton and Lagrange forms produce the same polynomial; they differ only in representation and numerical workflow.

Cases 01–29 below intentionally reuse the same interpolation cases as the [Lagrange page](../lagrange-polynomial-interpolation-and-approximation/index.qmd), matching the legacy Mathews case ordering; each case heading gives the function and the node interval $[a, b]$.

## Animations

Cases 01–29 each show the interpolant on 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16 equally spaced nodes (degree 1 to 5, then 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15) for a fixed function and node interval, with nodes at both ends of the interval. The degree in each title is the number of nodes minus one, the most the interpolant can have; its actual degree can be lower. With nodes symmetric about 0, the interpolant of an even $f$ has only even powers of $x$ and that of an odd $f$ only odd powers, so in the even cases (08, 13, 17, 20 and 22) the frame titled degree 1 is a horizontal line and the frame titled degree 15 has degree 14.

The shared script draws this same polynomial but evaluates it in the first barycentric (Lagrange) form, not by divided differences. The last case on this page has its own script, which builds the Newton form from divided differences.

[Julia source for Cases 01–29](lagnewt_animations_all.jl)

### Case 12: $f(x)=\sin x$, nodes on $[-3\pi, 3\pi]$

With 2, 3 and 4 nodes every node is a multiple of $\pi$, where $\sin x = 0$, so every divided difference is zero and the frames titled degree 1, 2 and 3 all show the line $y = 0$.

![Newton interpolating polynomials of f(x) = sin x through equally spaced nodes on [−3π, 3π], degree rising from 1 to 15, drawn with f on the same interval; at degrees 1, 2 and 3 every node is a multiple of π, so the interpolant is the line y = 0.](lagnewt12.gif)

### Case 13: $f(x)=\cos x$, nodes on $[-3\pi, 3\pi]$

With 2 and 4 nodes every node is an odd multiple of $\pi$, where $\cos x = -1$, so $a_0 = -1$, every later divided difference is zero, and the frames titled degree 1 and 3 show the line $y = -1$.

![Newton interpolating polynomials of f(x) = cos x through equally spaced nodes on [−3π, 3π], degree rising from 1 to 15, drawn with f on the same interval; at degrees 1 and 3 every node is an odd multiple of π, so the interpolant is the line y = −1.](lagnewt13.gif)

### Case 14: $f(x)=\tan x$, nodes on $[-1.45, 1.45]$

$\tan x$ is odd and the nodes are symmetric about 0, so the middle of three nodes, $(0, 0)$, lies on the line through the two end nodes. Hence $f[x_0, x_1, x_2] = 0$, and the frames titled degree 1 and 2 show the same line.

![Newton interpolating polynomials of f(x) = tan x through equally spaced nodes on [−1.45, 1.45], between the poles of f at x = ±π/2, degree rising from 1 to 15, drawn with f on [−π, π] and broken at its poles; the frames at degrees 1 and 2 show the same straight line.](lagnewt14.gif)

### Case 23: $f(x)=\tfrac12\left(1+\operatorname{erf}(x/\sqrt2)\right)$, nodes on $[-3, 3]$

$f(x)-\tfrac12$ is odd and the nodes are symmetric about 0, so the middle of three nodes, $(0, \tfrac12)$, lies on the line through the two end nodes. Hence $f[x_0, x_1, x_2] = 0$, and the frames titled degree 1 and 2 show the same line.

![Newton interpolating polynomials of the standard normal distribution function f(x) = ½(1 + erf(x/√2)) through equally spaced nodes on [−3, 3], degree rising from 1 to 15, drawn with f on the same interval; the frames at degrees 1 and 2 show the same straight line.](lagnewt23.gif)

### Divided differences: $f(x)=\cos x$, nodes $x_k = k/5$ on $[0, 1]$

**Behavior:** This is Mathews' Example 1. Each frame adds the next node $x_n = n/5$ and one more Newton term $a_n\prod_{j<n}(x-x_j)$; the coefficients already found do not change. The divided differences are $a_0,\ldots,a_5 = 1,\ -0.0996671,\ -0.488402,\ 0.0490076,\ 0.0381225,\ -0.00396205$. Between the first and last node (shaded) the largest error is $4.97\times10^{-3}$ at degree 1, $1.16\times10^{-4}$ at degree 2 and $1.35\times10^{-6}$ at degree 5, so there the curves coincide in the frames. The frames are drawn on $[-0.5, 2.1]$, as in Mathews' graphs, so each added term shows to the right of the nodes: the error at $x = 2.1$ falls from 1.30 at degree 1 to 0.65, 0.32, 0.067 and 0.015, and the degree-2 and degree-3 polynomials leave the bottom of the plot near $x = 1.81$ and $x = 1.95$.

[Julia source](newtpolyaa.jl)

![Newton interpolation of cos x with nodes x_k = k/5 on [0, 1] (Mathews' Example 1), adding one node per frame from degree 1 (2 nodes) to degree 5 (6 nodes), drawn on [−0.5, 2.1] with the interval [x_0, x_n] shaded; the dashed polynomial passes through every node, its largest error on the shaded interval falls from 4.97e-3 to 1.35e-6, and its gap from cos x to the right of the nodes shrinks from 1.30 to 0.015 at x = 2.1.](newtpolyaa.gif)
